title: By the mount and the book
hookLine: by the mount, and a book inscribed on open parchment (52:1–3)

cards: A young man from Mecca named Jubayr ibn Mut'im came to Medina after the battle of Badr, on business about prisoners. He wasn't a Muslim. At sunset he heard the Prophet ﷺ leading the prayer, reciting aloud.
Years later he described the moment, and his words are in Sahih al-Bukhari: when the recitation reached certain verses, my heart nearly flew. The surah he heard was At-Tur, the Mount.

teach.b: At-Tur, like Adh-Dhariyat, begins with oaths. Pickthall's translation: "By the Mount, And a Scripture inscribed On fine parchment unrolled."
The commentators understand the Mount, at-Tur, as Mount Sinai, where Musa heard Allah speak. The Arabic tur means a mountain, and in the Qur'an it points again and again to that one.
Then a book: kitabin mastur, written in lines, on raqqin manshur, parchment spread open. Raqq is fine, thin skin prepared for writing, kept for texts meant to last.
Which book? Commentators differ. Some say the Torah given at that mountain.
Some say the Qur'an. Some say the preserved tablet in heaven, or the records of deeds every person will see unrolled. The verse doesn't specify, and the scholars hold several views.
What's clear is the pairing: a mountain and a page. A place where revelation happened, and the writing that carries it to people who weren't there.
The oaths continue: by the frequented House, by the roof raised high, by the swelling sea. And they're answered: the punishment of your Lord will surely come.
Jubayr's heart nearly flew a little later in the surah, at verses that ask: were they created out of nothing, or are they the creators? A question, not an argument.
Reports say it was the first time faith settled in his heart, and he later became a Muslim. A recited page did that, in the half-light, to a man who came only for business.

how: Muslims handle the Qur'an with care: many perform ablution before touching the Arabic text, keep it on a high shelf, and say bismillah before reading; the Prophet's recitation of At-Tur in the sunset prayer is often followed by imams.

games.why: Bukhari records his words; reports say it was the start of his faith, and he later became Muslim.

practice: If there's a book you value near you, a Qur'an, a Bible, a book of poems, a family journal, bring it close; if not, picture one.

Before you open it, notice its weight, the cover, the edges of the pages, then open it slowly, as if it were parchment that might tear, and read one line. If you pray, you can say bismillah before you open it.

wordCard.voice: At-Tur: the Mount, understood as Mount Sinai where Musa heard Allah speak, the oaths that open this surah alongside a book written in lines on parchment spread open. Today's word.
